paragraphs.text: 4.	I am informed by [TextInput{"system-name":"informant-title-name-shield","label":"Title, Full Name, Shield"}] assigned to the [TextInput{"system-name":"informant-agency","label":"Agency"}]’s [TextInput{"system-name":"informant-assignment","label":"Assignment"}] [Select: Unit / Division / Bureau{"system-name":"unit-type"}] of the following: Mobile telephones are like sophisticated radios which work within a cellular network. “Cell sites,” “cell towers” or “base stations” are basically cellular transmitting and receiving stations which work like radio antennas. Cellular telephone networks are divided into “cells,” which are hexagon shaped coverage areas. Within each cell, there is an antenna tower referred to as a “cell site” or “cell tower” (or “base station”) which is basically a cellular transmitting and receiving station. Generally, every cell tower contains three directional antennas which divide the cell site into three 120 degree areas, one for each antenna. The coverage area of a particular cell depends on the area. When a mobile telephone is on, it is constantly scanning through the various base stations to find where it is getting the strongest signal or best reception. Once the telephone finds the strongest signal from a particular base station, the mobile telephone will identify itself by providing information about its service provider, and its unique identifiers such as ESN, IMSI, IMEI and/or MIN. These particular cell towers route and connect individual communications.  Generally, although not always, the strongest signal will come from the nearest cell site.  Mobile telephone carriers keep, in the regular course of their business, “call detail records,” which are records of all telephone calls placed and received by a mobile telephone, including telephone numbers dialed, and the origin of an incoming call, as well as the date, time and duration of a call, and the telephone numbers and other non-content transaction information associated with all SMS or MMS messages.  Mobile carriers also keep historical “cell site location information,” which are records of the location, site, and sector of the cell towers used at the beginning and end of these communications. Certain carriers, although not all, choose to maintain location estimates regarding where a device was in relation to a particular cell site as well as the approximate location of a device based on radio frequency measurements. Mobile telephone carriers do not keep records of cell sites used when a mobile telephone was merely on and not in use, or about the exact location of where a telephone was used in the past, or so-called “GPS” or “ping” information.  Rather, mobile telephone carriers only maintain more general cell site location information. Thus, historical cell site information shows the general vicinity of where a mobile telephone was operating during a particular time period in the past.
